info.name: ERP — Files & S3 key authorization
info.description:
Exercises the object-level guard added to /api/files/presign and /api/upload (docs/qa-audit-2026-08.md #5), plus the two findings still open.

Every request authenticates with a real NextAuth session cookie you paste into the `sessionToken` collection variable — see tests/postman/README.md for how to get it. `proxy.ts` does not match /api/*, so the cookie is the only thing standing between Postman and these routes.

Run the folders in order: 'Setup' harvests a real PO attachment key, 'Upload' harvests a key you own, and the presign folder uses both.

variable.description: next-auth v5 over http. Behind HTTPS it is __Secure-authjs.session-token.
Paste the cookie VALUE here (not name=value). See README.

exec: // Attach the session cookie to every request, except the one whose whole
// point is to arrive without it.
// The replace() is not decoration: a token copied out of a wrapped terminal
// line carries newlines, and a header value containing one is rejected with
console.warn('sessionToken is empty — every request will 401. See tests/postman/README.md');

request.description: Confirms the app is up and that you have the right baseUrl, before any auth question muddies the water.

item.name: PO list — proves the session cookie works, harvests a real attachment key

request.description:
A 401 here means the sessionToken variable is stale or wrong — fix that before reading anything into the presign results.

Saves the first attachment_key it finds into `poAttachmentKey`: a key that belongs to a row YOU can see, which is the positive case for the guard.

exec: console.warn('No PO in scope has an attachment — the in-scope presign test will be skipped.');

item.name: 1. Upload — keys are unguessable and stamped

formdata.description: Pick any PDF/PNG/CSV under 10 MB — Postman cannot pre-fill this.

request.description:
You must click 'Select Files' on the `file` row once — Postman will not interpolate a path there.

Asserts the returned key carries the -u<userId>-<12 hex> marker buildUploadKey adds. That marker is what lets you presign a file you just uploaded but haven't saved to any row yet (the Add Vendor / Add Manufacturer preview flow).

Note: this writes a real object to S3 under postman/qa/.

exec: pm.test('key is stamped with the uploader marker', () => {
pm.test('key keeps its folder and extension', () => {

item.name: Upload the same folder+field again — must not reuse the key

request.description: The overwrite half of audit #5. uploadFile is a plain PutObject, so the old predictable `${folder}/${field}.${ext}` key meant a second upload replaced the first object's bytes — an invoice PDF or vendor document could be swapped out underneath whatever referenced it. Identical inputs must now produce a different key.

exec: pm.test('a repeat upload cannot overwrite the first object', () => {

request.description: Rule 2 of assertKeyReadable: the marker in the key says you uploaded it, so it is readable even though no row references it yet. If this 403s, document previews in the Add Vendor / Add Manufacturer dialogs are broken.

item.name: My own key, inline view — allowed

request.description: Same guard, the view=1 branch, and confirms expiresIn is still clamped to 3600.

THE enumeration test. Before the fix this returned a working presigned URL for any key at all — so any signed-in user could walk the bucket using the attachment_key and csv_source_key values that ordinary list responses hand out. A key that resolves to no owning row must now be refused outright.

exec: pm.test('403, not a signed url', () => pm.response.to.have.status(403));
pm.test('no url leaked in the body', () => pm.expect(pm.response.text()).to.not.include('X-Amz-Signature'));

item.name: Someone else's marker on my key — 403

request.description: Takes your real uploaded key and rewrites the marker to user 999999. The marker no longer matches you, nothing owns the key, so it is refused — i.e. the marker grants access to your own uploads only, it is not a general bypass.

exec: pm.test('the rewritten key really is different', () => {

item.name: A real PO attachment I can see — allowed

request.description:
Rule 1: the key resolves to a purchase_orders row whose mfg_id and destination are in your scope. Skipped when no PO in your scope has an attachment.

This is the regression that matters most — if the owner lookup misses a table, real documents stop opening for everyone.

exec: pm.test.skip('no PO with an attachment in scope', () => {});
pm.test('a document on a PO I can see still opens', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

request.description: Unchanged behaviour — the guard runs after the required-param check, so a missing key is still a plain 400 and not a confusing 403.

The collection pre-request script skips the cookie for any request with 'no session' in its name. withGateway must reject before the guard is ever reached.

If Postman's own cookie jar has captured a cookie for this host, clear it (Cookies link under Send) or this will pass a session anyway.

item.name: 3. Still open — these SHOULD fail today
item.description: Red tests on purpose. They encode the desired behaviour for findings not yet fixed, so they flip green when the fix lands instead of needing to be remembered.

item.name: EXPECTED FAIL — preview of an unowned key (audit #5)

request.description:
/api/files/preview has the same hole presign had: it takes the key from the caller, parses whatever CSV/XLSX is at it, and returns the contents as JSON. Two lines away from fixed — assertKeyReadable, and delete the '..' check.

This asserts 403, so it fails until that lands. A 500 here means the object simply wasn't there, which is not authorization.

exec: pm.test('preview refuses a key owned by nothing', () => pm.response.to.have.status(403));

request.description:
supplier_invoices.mfg_id makes every invoice manufacturer-owned, but this route has no scope assertion — so ids can be walked. Informational here because proving it needs a user scoped to a DIFFERENT manufacturer than invoice 1's: signed in as an unrestricted user, a 200 is correct behaviour.

To turn this into a real test: create a user scoped to one manufacturer under /admin > Data Access, sign in as them, and re-run — a 200 on another manufacturer's invoice is the defect.

exec: console.log('invoice mfg_id =', pm.response.json().invoice.mfg_id, '— compare against your own entity scope');
